title_working: The Dot-com Bubble: How Get Big Fast Became a 78% Wipeout

paragraphs.text: On March 10, 2000, the Nasdaq Composite peaked at 5,048.62. At that moment, the index was worth more than double what it had been a year earlier.

spec.small: The all-time high of the dot-com era

paragraphs.text: The climb had been relentless. From January 1995 to that peak, the Nasdaq rose by about 579%. In 1999 alone, it gained 85.6%.

Then it broke. By October 2002, the Nasdaq had fallen to 1,114.11, a loss of 78% from its peak. This is the story of how a market convinced itself that profits could wait, and what happened when they could not.
The strategy of the era fit in three words: get big fast. Dot-com companies spent heavily on advertising to grab market share, betting that profits would follow the customers.

By January 2000, that spending reached the most expensive stage in American advertising. How many dot-com companies bought ads during Super Bowl XXXIV depends on whom you ask. Counts range from 12 to 19, depending on how a dot-com is defined.

spec.small: dot-com advertisers, depending on the definition

paragraphs.text: That same month, AOL and Time Warner announced a merger valued at $164 billion. Old media was buying into the new economy just weeks before the top.
The fall was not one crash but a long series of them. On April 14, 2000, the Nasdaq fell 9.7% in a single day, ending a week in which it lost 25.3%.
Pets.com, an online pet-supply store founded in 1998, had become famous for its sock-puppet mascot. On November 9, 2000, it went out of business, only nine months after its IPO.

spec.small: Out of business nine months after its IPO

paragraphs.text: The grocery-delivery startup Webvan collapsed in 2001. Boo.com, Toysmart.com and many others went from leaders of a revolution to failed companies.
Looking back, Gartner analyst Whit Andrews said the presumption that you needed to get big fast "worked for Amazon.com and virtually no one else."

spec.eyebrow: Whit Andrews, Gartner analyst, via CNET
spec.big: “…worked for Amazon.com and virtually no one else”
spec.small: On the presumption that you needed to get big fast

paragraphs.text: Pets.com, Webvan and Boo.com did not fail because the internet was a fad. They failed because they spent as if growth alone would pay the bills. Seen whole, the Nasdaq chart from those years is a mountain with a cliff on its far side. It was built by investors who stopped asking when a company would make money, and torn down when the market started asking again.
Every boom tells itself that this time is different. The numbers from 2000 suggest it rarely is.
